latin: Cicerō Fīlius. — Studeō, mī pater<sup>1</sup>, latīne audīre eā quae mihi tū dē ratiōne dīcendī graece trādidistī<sup>2</sup>, sī modo tibi est ōtium et sī vīs*.
Cicerō Pater. — An est, mī Cicerō, quod ego mālim*, quam tē quam doctissimum esse?
Ōtium autem prīmum est summum, quoniam aliquandō Rōma exeundī* potestās data est,
deinde ista tua studia vel maximīs<sup>3</sup> occupātiōnibus meīs anteferrem* libenter.
Fil. — Vīsne* igitur, ut<sup>4</sup> mē graece<sup>5</sup> solēs ōrdine interrogāre, sīc ego tē vicissim eīsdem<sup>6</sup> dē rēbus latīne interrogem.
Pat. — Sāne, sī placet. Sīc enim et ego tē meminisse* intellegam quae accēpistī, et tū ōrdine audiēs quae requīrēs...
Fil. — In quō est ipsa vīs ōrātōris?
Pat. — In rēbus et in verbīs. Sed et rēs et verba invenienda sunt et collocanda.
Vōx, mōtus, vultus, atque omnis āctiō ēloquendī comes<sup>7</sup> est; eārum rērum omnium cūstōs est memoriā...
Fil. — Quoniam igitur invenīre prīmum est ōrātōris, quid quaeret?
Pat. — Ut inveniat quem ad modum fidem faciat eīs quibus volet*<sup>8</sup> persuādēre<sup>9</sup>, et quem ad modum mōtum eōrum animīs adferat*...
Fil. — Testimōniōrum quae genera sunt?
Pat. — Dīvīnum et hūmānum. Dīvīnum est, ut ōrācula, auspicia, ut vāticinātiōnēs et respōnsa sacerdōtum<sup>10</sup>.
Hūmānum, quod spectātur ex auctōritāte, ex voluntāte, ex ōrātiōne aut lībera aut expressa<sup>11</sup> in quō īnsunt* scrīpta, pacta<sup>12</sup>, prōmissa, jūrāta, quaesīta<sup>13</sup>.
latinAccented: Cícerō Fī́lius. — Stúdeō, mī pater<sup>1</sup>, latī́ne audī́re eā quae mihi tū dē ratiṓne dīcéndī graece trādidístī<sup>2</sup>, sī modo tibi est ṓtium et sī vīs*.
Cícerō Pater. — An est, mī Cícerō, quod ego mālim*, quam tē quam doctíssimum esse?
Ṓtium autem prīmum est summum, quóniam aliquándō Rōma exeúndī* potéstās data est,
deínde ista tua stúdia vel máximīs<sup>3</sup> occupātiṓnibus meīs anteférrem* libénter.
Fil. — Vīsne* ígitur, ut<sup>4</sup> mē graece<sup>5</sup> solēs ṓrdine interrogā́re, sīc ego tē vicíssim eī́sdem<sup>6</sup> dē rēbus latī́ne intérrogem.
Pat. — Sāne, sī placet. Sīc enim et ego tē meminísse* intéllegam quae accēpístī, et tū ṓrdine áudiēs quae requī́rēs...
Fil. — In quō est ipsa vīs ōrātṓris?
Pat. — In rēbus et in verbīs. Sed et rēs et verba inveniénda sunt et collocánda.
Vōx, mōtus, vultus, atque omnis ā́ctiō ēloquéndī comes<sup>7</sup> est; eā́rum rērum ómnium cūstōs est memóriā...
Fil. — Quóniam ígitur invenī́re prīmum est ōrātṓris, quid quaeret?
Pat. — Ut invéniat quem ad modum fidem fáciat eīs quibus volet*<sup>8</sup> persuādḗre<sup>9</sup>, et quem ad modum mōtum eṓrum ánimīs ádferat*...
Fil. — Testimōniṓrum quae génera sunt?
Pat. — Dīvī́num et hūmā́num. Dīvī́num est, ut ōrā́cula, auspícia, ut vāticinātiṓnēs et respṓnsa sacerdṓtum<sup>10</sup>.
Hūmā́num, quod spectā́tur ex auctōritā́te, ex voluntā́te, ex ōrātiṓne aut lī́bera aut expréssa<sup>11</sup> in quō īnsunt* scrīpta, pacta<sup>12</sup>, prōmíssa, jūrā́ta, quaesī́ta<sup>13</sup>.
english: Cicero junior. — Papa, I am keen to hear from you in Latin what you have [told] (reported) me in Greek [about the principles of eloquence] (means of saying), if however [you have the time] (to you is leisure) and if you want.
Cicero senior. — Is there [anything], my [little] Cicero, that I could prefer [to seeing you] (that you be) as learned as possible?
As for time, [for the first time I have a great deal of it] (it is the more great), since at last the possibility [has been given me] of leaving Rome,
and [besides] (then) I would gladly put [your wishes] (these desires of yours) [in this matter] before (ante) even my most important occupations.
Son. — Do you want then, just as you are in the habit of questioning me in Greek [proceeding] in order, that I in my turn question you in Latin on these same [questions] (things)?

Father. — Certainly, if [it] pleases [you]. Thus in effect, [I will know] (will understand) if you have retained what you have [learnt] (received), and you will hear [set out] in order what you ask...
Son. — [Where lies the talent] (in what is the force itself) of the orator?
Father. — In the [ideas] (things) and in the words. But the ideas and the words must be found and [arranged] (are to be placed together).

The voice, [gesture] (movement), [the expression of the] face, [and] (all) [in general] (all) the action [of speaking] are the companion(s) [of elocution]; the guardian of all these things is memory...
Son. — So since [invention] (to find) is the first [aim] of the orator, what will he seek?
Father. — [To find] (that he may find) how to [convince] (make faith to) those whom he will want to persuade, and how [to move them] (movement to their souls he brings)...
Son. — What are the [different] kinds of testimonies?
Father. — The divine and the human. The divine [testimony] [is], for example, the oracles, the auspices, the predictions and the answers of the priests.

The human [testimony is] that which [comes] (is seen) from authority, from will, from speech free or forced; [in this category] (in which) are found writings, agreements, promises, oaths and [confessions obtained by torture] (things asked).

footnotes: Mi pater, is more familiar or more affectionate than pater mi, which simply means my father. Another example that shows that the place of words is not arbitrary in Latin (cf. R. and N. 84). Studere, to have the taste of... (studium, the taste of doing s.th.), whence to study; is constructed with the dative: studeo grammaticae, mathematicis, etc.
Trado, -is, -ere, tradidi, traditum, to hand over, to deliver, to report (trans do).

Vel + superlative, even the most. E.g.: vel minima sentire, to perceive the slightest things; compare with quam + superlative (P. 2 above). — Vel means or if you want (same etymology as velle*) and marks the NON-EXCLUSIVE or: Paulus vel Petrus venit, Paul or Pierre are coming (or perhaps they are both coming). — Aut, on the contrary, expresses the EXCLUSIVE or: Paulus aut Petrus venit, Paul or Pierre is coming; but if Pierre comes, Paul does not come and vice versa. It will be noticed that French and English do not have conjunctions clearly appropriate to each of these two logical operations, though they are so different from each other.
Ut is here an adverb of comparison (and not a conjunction). This becomes evident if one notices that it makes a pair with sic.
Graece, adv.: the usual language of teaching was Greek before being Latin.

Vicissim, adv., in turn; from vix (a word only used in a few cases: acc. vicem, gen. vicis, nom. and acc. pl. vices, dat. and abl. pl. vicibus), turn, time, succession: in vicem, in turn (cf. French vicissitude, vice versa, vice-amiral, etc.).
Comes, -itis, m. f., companion; this word became a title in the Lower Empire: whence the French comte and the Italian conte.
Volet: future indicative of velle*. Higher up (P. 2) malim, subj. pres. of malle*.
Suadeo, -es, -ere, suasi, suasum, to persuade; persuadere means to persuade completely; is constructed with the dative (quibus).

Oraculum, -i, n., from orare, to speak, then to pray; oracula are the words of an inspired soothsayer. — Auspicium, -ii, n. (avis spicium, from aves inspicere), prophecies obtained by examining the flight of birds (avis, -is, f., and, in classical writing, auis). — Vaticinatio, -onis, f., prophecies. Vates, -is, m., the prophet or the poet; in effect, many ancient poets were considered as prophets (e.g. Virgil, who predicted the future of Rome and even, according to some, that of Christianity); moreover, prophetic formulas were often in verse. — Sacerdos, -otis, m. f., priest(ess); from sacer, -cra, -crum, sacred.
Exprimo, -is, -ere, pressi, pressum, to press (premere) to make something come out (cf. to express the juice of a fruit).
Paciscor, -eris, -i, pactus sum, to make a pact; this verb can be transitive: quid pacti sumus?, what have we agreed on?
Quaesita (from quaerere, to seek) is what one obtains by the quaestio, -onis, f., the question, which was sometimes put by more efficacious means than the simple verbal request!
comments: Verecundus, -a, -um, modest; modestus means moderate (modus); the corresponding nouns are verecundia, modesty, and modestia, moderation. — Dissentire, to feel differently. — Disputastis = disputavistis; disputare means to discuss (comes from putare, to think) and not to quarrel.

latin: Cūr tacēs? Nōnne domī meae ōtiō lēniter frueris?
Hīc ōtiō lēnissimē fruor.
Vōs autem summā voluptāte audiō quī dē rēbus ad dēlectātiōnem aptīs tam disertē colloquimini.
Nōs colloquentēs irrīdēs.
Immō! Verēcundiōrēs estis. Ambō pertinenter et nōnnunquam facētē locūtī estis.
Nōnnūllīs tamen in quibus dissēnsimus exceptīs! — Ad Foederātārum Nātiōnum Societātem pertinentibus.
In verbīs modo dissensistis; rē vērā sententia nostra eadem est: in terrā pāx hominibus bonae voluntātis!
Dē viīs tantum ad pācem condendam cōnfirmandamque disputāvimus.
Tālī modo ante bellum praeteritum disputastis (Assimil Germānicum, L. 101).
Timeō nē bellum vītārī nōn possit*: homō hominī lupus.
Ā sententiā tuā omnīnō dissentiō: ex illō tempore in viā bonā multum prōgressī sumus.
latinAccented: Cūr tacēs? Nōnne domī meae ṓtiō lḗniter frúeris?
Hīc ṓtiō lēníssimē fruor.
Vōs autem summā voluptā́te áudiō quī dē rēbus ad dēlectātiṓnem aptīs tam disértē colloquímini.
Nōs colloquéntēs irrī́dēs.
Immō! Verēcundiṓrēs estis. Ambō pertinénter et nōnnúnquam facḗtē locū́tī estis.
Nōnnū́llīs tamen in quibus dissḗnsimus excéptīs! — Ad Foederātā́rum Nātiṓnum Societā́tem pertinéntibus.
In verbīs modo dissensístis; rē vērā senténtia nostra éadem est: in terrā pāx homínibus bonae voluntā́tis!
Dē viīs tantum ad pācem condéndam cōnfirmandámque disputā́vimus.
Tālī modo ante bellum praetéritum disputástis (Ássimil Germā́nicum, L. 101).
Tímeō nē bellum vītā́rī nōn possit*: homō hóminī lupus.
Ā senténtiā tuā omnī́nō disséntiō: ex illō témpore in viā bonā multum prōgréssī sumus.
english: Why don't you say anything? [Aren't you having a good time] at my place (of a tranquil leisure gently you profit)?
Here I am spending a very good time.
For I listen to you with the greatest pleasure, [you] who converse so brilliantly about subjects [full of charm] (suited to delectation).
You are making fun of us (conversing).
On the contrary! You are too modest. Both of you have spoken judiciously and sometimes with wit.
Except for a few [points] (in which) [we were not in agreement]! — On the subject of the [Organisation] (association) of the United Nations.
[It is] only on the words [that] you were not in agreement; [in reality] (by true thing) our opinion is the same: peace on earth to men of good will!
We only discussed the [means] (ways) of establishing and maintaining peace.
You discussed in the same way before the last war (German Assimil, L. 101).
I fear that war cannot be avoided: man is a wolf to man.
I am not at all in agreement [with you] (with your opinion): since that time we have made great progress on the right path.
